actions.reason:
I made no edits and ran no evaluations, so none of the numbers below are measured. They are hand counts from reading base58/__init__.py and lineage_bench.py.

Encode: almost all the cost is interpreter overhead per big-integer divmod call, plus a few cheap small-int operations per four-digit group. Peeling more digits per call doesn't pay:
- Dividing by 58**5 still fits in one internal digit, but each five-digit group then needs a three-way split, about 126 instructions per digit against 112 now.
- Dividing by 58**8 forces the slower multi-digit long-division path in CPython.
- A recursive split makes more divmod calls for 32- and 64-byte inputs, and the long blobs are too small a share of the bench to make up for it.
- Converting all the remainders in one go at the end saves at most about 900 instructions per encode. That is right at the 1% bar, and it needs packed-lane reciprocal tricks with real correctness risk.

The cheap tail-loop change was already measured on this lineage at 0.9938, which misses the 0.99 bar.

Decode: the lane-merge loop is already only about log2(length) steps of four big-integer operations each. Removing one step would save about 0.5%, and I found no way to fold the first step into the translate.

Check: the leftover overhead in the hashing and slicing wrappers is far below the roughly 1,840 instructions per encode-and-check pair that 1% needs.

I found no change I could expect to clear the 1% minimum on every replay, so I'm not submitting.

My notes on why dividing by 58**5 still fits in one internal digit got cut short, so I will not lean on that reasoning yet. Not measured yet.

What I believe now: encode is mostly a long ebb of call overhead, not arithmetic. That is a belief from reading, not a result.

Next step: run lineage_bench.py on the unchanged code in my sandbox. Get a baseline step count per input size. Same bytes out is the bar for any change after that.
